# ligthart-2025-reconsidering-absolute-nature
- **URL:** https://academic.oup.com/hrlr/article/25/3/ngaf018/8155294 (OA PDF read from https://research-portal.uu.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/266452493/ngaf018.pdf) · **Accessed:** 2026-09-16 · **For:** v1 response round, finding (b) "Ligthart argues the absolute right must admit implied limitations"
- **Citation:** Sjors Ligthart, "Reconsidering the absolute nature of the right to freedom of thought," *Human Rights Law Review* 25:3 (2025), ngaf018, https://doi.org/10.1093/hrlr/ngaf018 (published online 2 June 2025; issue Sept. 2025). PDF page N = journal page N−1.
- **What it establishes:** Editor's characterization holds, with two attribution corrections. (1) The "evidently false" line is Ligthart *quoting Bublitz* (n. 41 → Bublitz, "Freedom of Thought in the Age of Neuroscience," 100 ARSP 1 (2014), at 6). (2) "Categorical insistence … is unpersuasive" is prefaced "I agree with Bublitz that…" (n. 149 → Bublitz, "Freedom of Thought as an International Human Right," in Blitz & Bublitz eds., *The Law and Ethics of Freedom of Thought*, at 90). So the relativizing move is Bublitz-then-Ligthart, not Ligthart alone. Three implied limitations proposed; an absolute "essence" retained (no punishment for thoughts alone; no coerced disclosure of moral/political views; no non-consensual imprinting of moral/political views).
- **Key passages:**
  - Abstract: "It is often assumed that the right protects these freedoms in an absolute way. This article challenges the assumption that the RFoT is completely absolute in established human rights law. Furthermore, it is submitted that the right—as currently understood in the literature—neither should be constructed, completely, in absolute terms."
  - p. 5 (§2.B "Inner thoughts are beyond state power"): "these suffice to refute the premise that inner thoughts are factually and epistemically beyond the reach of third parties like state officials. As Bublitz writes, this premise is 'evidently false'. Rather, '[m]odern day Leviathan would be able to peer into the brains and minds of citizens and possesses the tools to alter thoughts, beliefs and convictions, and most governments at least sometimes do so.'"
  - p. 18 (§3.A "Revitalization through Relativization"): "Against this background, I agree with Bublitz that categorical insistence on the absolute nature of the RFoT—prohibiting any interference in every case—is unpersuasive." Also quotes O'Callaghan & Shiner: the "prevailing view … is that although it is symbolically important, it is of little or no practical significance."
  - p. 21 (§3.C): "Whether it also provides a compelling argument to exclude any exception to this rule—even in very specific emergency situations, aiming to save lives or prevent torture—can however be challenged."
  - p. 23 (§4 "Absolute safeguards: the essence of the RFoT"): "One way to guarantee absolute safeguards to core aspects of non-absolute rights is through the essence of rights doctrine."
  - p. 25: "Any (impeding) possibility of punishing people simply for what they think plausibly restricts free thinking in general." … "Coercing people to reveal their moral or political views may have a chilling effect on free thinking in general. It may restrict people in exploring, developing, or changing such views."
  - p. 26 (Conclusion): interference with the freedom against alteration "may, perhaps, be justified in specific cases when necessary and proportionate (1) to restore or enhance the right-holder's freedom to think while the person themselves is incompetent to give free and informed consent to the interference, or (2) to prevent imminent and severe harm to the person themselves or others. Furthermore, perhaps, (3) interference with the freedom not to reveal thoughts could be permissible when necessary and proportionate to prevent severe imminent harm to others, also beyond the context of patient care (such as in emergency situations to save lives or prevent torture)."
- **Reliability:** Primary, peer-reviewed, CC-BY. Ligthart is a co-author of the Tesink et al. extended-mind paper (see tesink note), so his positions on absoluteness and on extension are consistent within one school.
- **Relevance to this project:** The essay's opening "no limitations whatsoever" stance must acknowledge that the leading current treatment (Bublitz → Ligthart) argues for implied limitations while keeping an absolute core. Usefully, the retained core (no coerced disclosure of moral/political views; chilling of "exploring, developing, or changing" views) is exactly the function the essay assigns to the externalized forum internum.
- **Addendum 2026-09-16 (v2→v3 response round, slice M / M1) — re-read of the OA PDF (research-portal.uu.nl … ngaf018.pdf; journal p. = PDF p. − 1):**
  - **Section correction to this note:** "Against this background, I agree with Bublitz that categorical insistence on the absolute nature of the RFoT—prohibiting any interference in every case—is unpersuasive." is at journal **p. 18, inside §3.B "Altering thoughts: treating patients in mental healthcare"** (heading at p. 16), not §3.A as recorded above. The review's "§3.B" is right.
  - **Citation chain:** n. 149 = "Bublitz supra n 16 at 90"; n. 16 = "Cf. Bublitz, 'Freedom of Thought as an International Human Right', in Blitz and Bublitz supra n 2"; n. 2 lists *both* "Blitz and Bublitz (eds.), The Law and Ethics of Freedom of Thought, Volume 1 (2022)" and "Bublitz and Blitz (eds.), The Law and Ethics of Freedom of Thought, Vol. 2 (in press)". The editor order "Blitz and Bublitz" = **Volume 1**. Crossref confirms: Bublitz, "Freedom of Thought as an International Human Right: Elements of a Theory of a Living Right," in *Volume 1* (Palgrave 2021), pp. 49–101, doi 10.1007/978-3-030-84494-3_3 — so "at 90" fits; and vol. 2's ten chapters (see bublitz-2026-what-is-thought) contain no such chapter. **The review's claim that Ligthart cites it "as in press in vol. 2" is wrong**; only the volume as a whole is cited "in press" in n. 2.
  - **"Absolute essence" list — location correction:** the single-sentence list is in **§5 Conclusion, p. 27**, not §4. Verbatim (layout-mode extraction): "this article tentatively suggested that respecting the essence of the RFoT requires no punishment for unexpressed thought; no use of force to reveal a person's political or moral views; nor the imprinting of such views into persons' minds, especially not through means that undermine or bypass the person's (mental) autonomy." §4 (pp. 23–25) develops the same three as numbered "candidate examples": "1. Freedom from impermissible alteration of thought", "2. Freedom from force to reveal unmanifested thoughts", "3. Freedom from punishment for thoughts" — prefaced "An in-depth analysis of the essence of the RFoT is beyond the scope of this article. But let me provide some tentative suggestions that may spark further debate." (p. 24). Note the hedges: "tentatively", "candidate examples".
